thread.title: Spotify IPO: 5 things to know about the streaming-music giant’s direct listing - MarketWatch

author: Emily Bary
title: Spotify IPO: 5 things to know about the streaming-music giant’s direct listing - MarketWatch
text:
Nearly a year to the day after Snap Inc.’s initial public offering, investors got a glimpse at what’s likely to be the biggest public tech debut since Snapchat’s parent company premiered.
Music-streaming service Spotify Technology SA SPOT, +0.00% filed Wednesday for a direct listing, revealing for the first time details of its steepening losses, fast-growing user base and ever-more-popular family plans.
Spotify is expected to make a big splash when its shares begin trading, even though the process by which the company goes public will be different than what investors are used to. Spotify won’t issue new shares and will forgo and a traditional initial public offering, opting for a direct listing instead. It’s an unusual move that could set a new standard for hot tech companies looking for an IPO alternative.
Opinion: The Spotify IPO filing includes a giant warning sign
The company won’t conduct the usual roadshow, but it will still have to convince investors to look past its deep losses. Given a general lack of big tech IPOs, that might not be hard. Investors eager to get in on the action sent shares of Snap SNAP, +3.37% and Roku Inc. ROKU, -3.34% soaring after those firms made their public launches. Spotify has reportedly fetched a private-market valuation of nearly $20 billion .
Here are five key takeaways from Spotify’s filing.
The raw numbers
Spotify generated revenue of €4.09 billion ($4.99 billion) last year, up from €2.95 billion the year prior, for growth of 39%. The company’s losses, however, more than doubled, reaching €1.24 billion in 2017 versus €539 million in 2016.
“We have incurred significant operating losses in the past, and we may not be able to generate sufficient revenue to be profitable, or to generate positive cash flow on a sustained basis,” the company said in its filing. “In addition, our revenue growth rate may decline.”
The public debut
Direct listings are different from traditional initial public offerings in that a company doesn’t issue new shares or seek to raise money through the process of going public. Rather, the listing makes it possible for existing shareholders to sell their shares to the public. This helps cut down on costs for the firm going public, which then doesn’t have to pay banks to underwrite an offering. It also prevents a company from dealing with share lockups or share dilution, two areas that can frustrate firms that hold startups’ shares before an IPO.
Don’t miss: Five ways tech startups are avoiding IPOs
Were Spotify’s direct listing to be a success, it could set a precedent for other big tech firms seeking to go public while avoiding some of the IPO headaches. However, the process is not without risk. Spotify warned in the risk-factors section of its filing that listing doesn’t have “the same safeguards as an underwritten initial public offering, which may result in the public price of our ordinary shares being volatile and declining significantly upon listing.”
The competition
Whereas music streaming is just a tiny part of Apple Inc.’s AAPL, -0.39% overall business, it’s all Spotify does. Spotify calls out Apple Music early on in its form F-1 filing, saying that it believes its own paid service “has nearly double the scale of our closest competitor, Apple Music.” The company’s tight focus could help it more easily come up with new features and services that please users, as Spotify doesn’t have to deal with internal politics derailing music initiatives the way a much larger firm (that does music on the side) might.
That said, Spotify also doesn’t have a sizable and highly profitable hardware business to help pay the bills for music initiatives, the way Apple does, or a sizable and highly profitable display-ad business the way Alphabet Inc. GOOGL, -0.15% does. (Alphabet’s YouTube has cycled through many variants of music-streaming services and is expected to roll out a new one soon .)
Of course, there is a public company that specifically focuses solely on music, but Spotify likely wants to avoid all comparisons to it. Pandora Media Inc. P, +3.53% the streaming-music pioneer, has yet to turn an annual profit and has seen net losses widen in recent years as it struggles to find an identity in the on-demand age. Pandora’s saga illustrates that music-streaming companies may never be able to turn a profit due to the costs required for music as well as the competitive landscape.
Loyal users
One thing Spotify has that Pandora doesn’t is a rapidly growing user base. (Pandora has seen listener hours decline .) Spotify had 71 million paying users at the end of 2017, up from 48 million in 2016. Overall monthly active users, which includes paid and free users, totaled 159 million compared with 123 a year earlier. Churn, a measure of users leaving the service, continues to fall, hitting 5.5% in 2017.

That stickiness suggests that Spotify might have some leverage if it wishes to raise prices down the line. Loyal users who have built up a library of music and grown accustomed to the company’s personalized playlists may not want to replicate that library on a rival service.
Family plans
Spotify’s average revenue per Premium user has been falling, and the company says that family plans are a big reason why. When up to six people pack onto a $15-a-month combined plan, they’re all counted as users, but they’re paying far less than they would have for individual memberships that cost $10 a month. Spotify’s average revenue per Premium user dropped to €5.32 last year, from €6.20 the year before, but the company says that family plans are a key reason why churn rates are improving.
“With the growth in higher retention products, such as our Family Plan and Student Plan, we believe these trends will continue in the future,” the filing said.
